Status: built 25 Oct 2026 from Upgraded Copy; copy still marked 'awaiting owner review'. AI imagery carries a 'Concept image' label.

## Instagram
Track saw in the van, or panels arriving cut and edged? Most fitters we speak to do a bit of both.

A: Cutting your own
Good for last-minute changes and one-off scribes. The catch is time, and keeping long cuts straight and corners square on a portable setup, especially across a full 2440 x 1220 sheet.

B: Ordering cut and edged panels
Panels come off a sliding table panel saw and an edge bander, so they arrive square with the ABS edging already applied. The catch is that you need a final cutting list before you order. Change your mind on site and you are back to option A.

Plenty of trade customers split it: carcass panels and long runs ordered in, fillers and scribes cut on site.

Which way do you work, and what is the one job that always makes you switch? Tell us in the comments.

## Facebook
A question for the joiners, fitters and cabinet makers who follow us around Stoke-on-Trent: do you cut your own boards, or have them sent out cut and edged?

Cutting your own gives you room to adjust when a wall is not quite what the drawing said. Ordering in saves hours at the saw and gives you square panels with the edging already on, but it only works with a final cutting list.

A lot of people do both: carcasses ordered in, fillers cut on site. What is your split? Let us know below, and if you fancy trying it with your next job, the details are here:

## Facebook
A question we hear from trade customers most weeks: if I send you a cutting list, how do I know it will fit?

The honest answer is that a square, accurate cut is only as good as the list behind it. A few habits make all the difference:
• Give finished sizes, length then width, every time
• Mark which edges get ABS edging (0.4, 1 or 2 mm)
• Show grain direction on oak-effect and woodgrain boards
• Name the board, colour and thickness

We look over lists before they go to the saw and query anything that does not add up. Ask us for a priced cutting list here:
https://superiofurniture.com/panel-cutting/?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=autumn-interiors-and-practical-comfort&utm_content=day-049

## Google Business Profile
How do I make sure cut panels fit my job?

It is the most common question from trade customers sending work to our Hanley workshop. Panels are cut on a sliding table panel saw and checked for squareness, but the fit on site depends just as much on the cutting list.

For the best result:
- List finished sizes, length first, then width
- Mark which edges need ABS edging, in 0.4, 1 or 2 mm
- Show grain direction on oak-effect and woodgrain boards
- State the board type, colour and thickness

We look over every list before cutting and query anything that does not add up, such as a door wider than its opening or a shelf deeper than its carcass. We can also drill hinge cups and shelf-pin rows and assemble cabinets, so panels arrive ready for the next stage.

Joiners, fitters and cabinet makers across Stoke-on-Trent and Staffordshire are welcome to send a list for a priced breakdown. Trade and domestic orders welcome.

## Instagram
One badly placed socket can push a whole media unit off-centre. That is why we note them first.

When we come out for a design consultation, a surprising amount of time goes on the boring bits:

• Sockets and switches: where they sit decides where a TV unit, desk or worktop appliance can go, and whether a drawer will clash with a plug.
• Radiators: fitted furniture in front of one traps heat, so the layout has to leave it room or plan around it.
• Skirting height: it decides whether units are scribed over it or the skirting is cut back.
• Window boards and reveals: they set how close a tall unit can sit.

Spotting these at the start means fewer compromises later, and an itemised quote that reflects the real room rather than a perfect box.

Which of these is the awkward one in your room? Tell us below and we will say how we would handle it.

## Facebook
Here is something people do not expect from a design consultation: we spend a good while looking at your sockets.

It sounds dull, but a socket in the wrong place can push a media unit off-centre, stop a drawer opening, or leave a plug stuck behind a cupboard. Radiators, skirting boards and window reveals are the same story. Noting them at the first visit means the design works around your actual room, not an ideal one.

Status: built 25 Oct 2026 from Upgraded Copy; copy still marked 'awaiting owner review'. AI imagery carries a 'Concept image' label.

## Instagram
Most kitchens are not short of cupboards. They are short of the right things in the right place.

Planning a kitchen in storage zones is the simplest way to fix that. Think about the order you actually work in:

1. Food storage: larder, fridge and dry goods together.
2. Crockery and cutlery: within one step of the dishwasher.
3. Cleaning: sink, bin and products as one unit of space.
4. Preparation: the longest clear worktop, ideally between sink and hob, with knives and boards in the drawers below.
5. Cooking: pans, oils and utensils right next to the hob.

Get the order right and you stop crossing the room with a dripping colander or a stack of plates. It is the foundation of every bespoke kitchen layout we plan, whatever the size of the room.

Save this before you start looking at door colours. Layout first, finishes second. When you are ready, the link in bio takes you to our kitchens page.

## Facebook
Here is a simple test for your kitchen: how many steps does it take to unload the dishwasher? If the answer involves walking to the other side of the room, your storage is working against you.

When we plan a bespoke kitchen, we start with five zones: food, crockery, cleaning, prep and cooking, laid out in the order you work. Pans by the hob, plates by the dishwasher, bin by the sink. It sounds obvious, but most kitchens grow without a plan and end up muddled.

## Instagram
Put the plates one step from the dishwasher and unloading stops being a chore.

Of all the storage zones in a kitchen, crockery and cutlery get used the most. Yet in a lot of kitchens they sit on the far side of the room, so every unload is a walk back and forth with stacked plates.

The fix is simple to plan:
• Cutlery drawer with an insert directly beside the dishwasher
• Everyday plates and bowls in a deep drawer just below, so you lift them out rather than reaching up
• Glasses and mugs in the nearest wall unit or a tall unit next to it

The best-loved items get the best spot. Serving dishes and the Christmas platter can live further away.

Is your cutlery drawer near the dishwasher, or on the other side of the kitchen? Tell us in the comments.

Small detail, big difference: where is your cutlery drawer in relation to the dishwasher?

If it is across the room, you will know the shuffle: one handful of forks at a time, then back for the plates. When we plan a bespoke kitchen, the crockery and cutlery zone goes right next to the dishwasher, with a cutlery insert in the top drawer and deep drawers for everyday plates below. ## Instagram
Before a single door colour is chosen, the zones go down on paper. Here is how that mapping works.

This is the planning sequence we follow for a kitchen layout, and you can try the first few steps yourself this weekend:

1. List what you own. Be honest about the air fryer.
2. Mark the anchors: sink, hob and fridge.
3. Draw the five zones around them in the order you work.
4. Choose the storage type for each zone: drawers for heavy things, tall units for food, a pull-out bin by the sink.
5. Look for clashes: doors that collide, drawers that block the dishwasher, dead corners.
6. Cook a meal on the drawing. If you cross the room twice, something is in the wrong place.

With the clocks going back tomorrow night, the kitchen is about to get busier in the evenings, so it is a good time to notice what slows you down.

Save this, try steps one and two, and bring your notes to a free consultation. Link in bio.

## Facebook
Planning a new kitchen? Here is a job you can do before anyone comes round, and it costs nothing.

Grab a sheet of paper, sketch where the sink, hob and fridge sit, then list everything that lives in your kitchen. Next, group it: food, crockery, cleaning, prep and cooking. You will quickly see where things are stored miles from where they are used.

# DAY-069 (2026-11-01) Engagement / inspiration post — Instagram + Facebook
Topic: Sliding versus hinged wardrobe doors
Status: built 25 Oct 2026 from Upgraded Copy; copy still marked 'awaiting owner review'. AI imagery (AI-18, AI-19) carries a 'Concept image' label.

## Instagram
Your wardrobe faces the bed with a modest gap between them. Which doors would you live with?

This is the most common layout we are asked about, and both choices have a cost.

A: Sliding doors
They never swing into the room, so the walkway stays clear even with the doors open. The cost: you only see part of the wardrobe at a time, and internal drawers have to be planned around the overlap.

B: Hinged doors
Open two doors and the whole wardrobe is in front of you, with drawers wherever you want them. The cost: each door needs clear floor to swing, so a tight gap means doors that knock the bed or a shuffle to get past.

There is no wrong answer, just the trade-off you would rather live with every morning.

A or B? Tell us the rough gap you have and what you mostly store, and we will tell you which we would lean towards.

## Facebook
Here is a bedroom puzzle a lot of people will recognise: the wardrobe is on the wall facing the bed, and the gap between them is not huge.

Sliding doors keep that walkway clear, but you only ever open half the wardrobe. Hinged doors open everything up, but need room to swing. Neither is wrong, it just depends on which compromise suits you.

Which would you choose, A or B? Pop your answer and the rough gap you have in the comments, and we will give you our honest take. See our fitted wardrobes here:

# DAY-070 (2026-11-02) FAQ / trust post — Facebook + Google Business Profile
Topic: Sliding versus hinged wardrobe doors
Status: built 25 Oct 2026 from Upgraded Copy; copy still marked 'awaiting owner review'. AI imagery carries a 'Concept image' label.

## Facebook
One of the questions we get most from people in older houses: 'Our bedroom floor is not level. Can we still have sliding wardrobe doors?'

Usually, yes. Sliding doors depend on level tracks rather than a level floor, so the floor and ceiling are checked at the survey, and the tracks are set level when we fit. Uneven walls are dealt with using scribed fillers, cut to follow the line of the wall.

If your floor has a serious slope, mention it at the consultation, as it can change which doors we would suggest. Ask your question or arrange a visit here:
https://superiofurniture.com/contact/?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=autumn-interiors-and-practical-comfort&utm_content=day-070

## Google Business Profile
Will sliding wardrobe doors work if my floor is not level?

In most homes, yes. Sliding doors depend on level tracks rather than a perfectly level floor. At the survey we check the floor and ceiling, and on fitting day our own team sets the top and bottom tracks level and adjusts each door so it runs smoothly and meets evenly.

Walls that are out of true are handled with scribed fillers, cut to follow the wall so there are no gaps along the edge. Sloping ceilings can be built around too, although they sometimes make hinged doors the more practical choice.

If your bedroom floor has a noticeable slope, it is worth mentioning at the free, no-obligation design consultation so we can talk through the options. SUPERIO fitted wardrobes are made in our Hanley workshop and fitted across Stoke-on-Trent and Staffordshire.

Topic: Concealing cables and equipment

## Instagram
Hidden cables are planned before the unit is built, not tidied up after it is fitted.

If you are planning a media wall or TV unit this winter, settle these five things first:

1. List every device. Soundbar, router, console, set-top box: each needs power, a route and a shelf it fits on.
2. Put sockets where the kit lives. Your electrician can place them behind the TV and inside the equipment area before anything is fitted.
3. Plan the cable route. A void behind the back panel and cable holes in the right places carry everything out of sight.
4. Let it breathe. Closed cupboards need ventilation gaps or slatted fronts, because equipment gets warm.
5. Think about signal. Solid doors can block remotes and weaken Wi-Fi.

Get these right at the design stage and there is nothing to hide later.

Save this for when you start planning, and find our media walls through the link in bio.

## Facebook
With darker evenings and more time on the sofa, the tangle of cables under the TV starts to get noticed.

The secret to a media wall with no visible cables is simple: it is planned before anything is built. List your devices, get sockets placed where the equipment will sit, design a route behind the unit, and think about airflow and remote signals for anything hidden behind doors.
